title: Models, ViewData, and ViewBag
description: Understand how models represent data in ASP.NET Core MVC, and learn when and how to use ViewData and ViewBag for passing supplementary data from controllers to views.

blocks.text: In the MVC pattern, **models** represent your application's data and business rules. A model is simply a C# class with properties — sometimes called a **Plain Old CLR Object (POCO)** because it does not depend on ASP.NET Core or any specific framework.

When a controller needs to send data to a view, it has three options: pass a strongly typed model, use `ViewData` (a dictionary), or use `ViewBag` (a dynamic wrapper around `ViewData`). Each approach has different tradeoffs.
A model class is a plain C# class that represents an entity in your application. It contains properties that describe the data, and optionally methods that implement business logic or validation.

blocks.content: A simple model class with properties representing a product.

blocks.title: Computed properties
blocks.text: C# lets you define properties without a backing field using expression-bodied members (`=>`). The `IsAvailable` and `DisplayPrice` properties are computed on demand — they do not store data, they calculate it from other properties.
Passing a Strongly Typed Model to a View

The most common way to pass data to a view is with a strongly typed model. The controller creates or retrieves the model object and passes it to `View(model)`. The view declares the type with `@model` and accesses properties directly.

blocks.content: Pass a Product model from the controller to the Details view.

blocks.content: The Details.cshtml view declares the model type and uses it to render the product.

blocks.text: `ViewData` is a dictionary (`Dictionary<string, object>`) that lives for the duration of a single request. It is useful for passing small supplementary values that do not warrant a dedicated model property, such as a page title or a notification message.

blocks.title: Using ViewData for a page title
blocks.content: Set ViewData in the controller and read it in the view.

blocks.title: ViewData values must be cast
blocks.text: Because `ViewData` stores values as `object`, you must cast them to the correct type when reading them back. Forgetting to cast will cause runtime errors.
`ViewBag` is a dynamic wrapper around `ViewData`. It provides the same functionality but with a cleaner syntax — no casting required when reading values.

blocks.title: Using ViewBag for supplementary data
blocks.content: Set ViewBag values in the controller and read them without casting in the view.

blocks.text: Since `ViewBag` and `ViewData` share the same underlying dictionary, setting `ViewBag.Title = "Hi"` is the same as setting `ViewData["Title"] = "Hi"`. They are two syntaxes for the same data store.

blocks.title: Strongly Typed Model vs. ViewData vs. ViewBag

cards.title: Strongly Typed Model
cards.description: Pass a typed object to View(model). The view declares @model for full compile-time safety.
pros: Self-documenting — the view declares what data it needs

cards.title: ViewData
cards.description: A Dictionary<string, object> for passing data. Values are stored as objects and require casting.
pros: Good for simple one-off values like titles
cons: Typos in keys cause runtime errors

cards.title: ViewBag
cards.description: A dynamic wrapper around ViewData. Same data store with cleaner syntax and no casting.

blocks.title: When to use each
items: **Strongly typed model** — Use for the primary data displayed on a page (the product, the order, the user profile)
**ViewBag** — Use for supplementary values like page titles, notification messages, or flags
**ViewData** — Use when you need a dictionary-like collection of values, but ViewBag is usually preferred

terms.definition: Plain Old CLR Object — a simple C# class without dependencies on specific frameworks. Models are typically POCOs for maximum flexibility.
A Dictionary<string, object> that passes data from controller to view for the duration of a single HTTP request. Values must be cast when read.
A dynamic wrapper around ViewData that provides the same functionality with cleaner syntax and no casting required.
A view that declares @model with a specific type, enabling IntelliSense, compile-time checking, and safer code.

blocks.title: Pass Data to a View Three Ways
blocks.description: Practice using strongly typed models, ViewBag, and ViewData in the same controller action.
steps: In ProductsController, create a new action called `Summary(int id)`
Retrieve a product by ID from the static list, or return NotFound()
Pass the product as a strongly typed model using `return View(product)`
Set `ViewBag.PageTitle` to the product name in the same action
Set `ViewData["ItemCount"]` to the total number of products in the list
Create `Summary.cshtml` in Views/Products that reads the model, ViewBag.PageTitle, and ViewData["ItemCount"]
Run the app and visit `/Products/Summary/1` to confirm all three data sources appear
blocks.expectedOutcome: The Summary page displays the product name from the model, a page title from ViewBag, and the total item count from ViewData — all three data-passing methods working together.

blocks.title: Lesson Summary
points: Models are plain C# classes (POCOs) that represent application data and business rules
Strongly typed views use @model to declare the expected data type, enabling IntelliSense and compile-time safety
ViewData is a Dictionary<string, object> for passing supplementary data between controller and view
ViewBag is a dynamic wrapper around ViewData with cleaner syntax and no casting
ViewBag and ViewData share the same underlying dictionary — they are two syntaxes for the same data
Prefer strongly typed models for primary page data; use ViewBag for simple supplementary values
blocks.takeaway: Passing data from controllers to views is fundamental to every ASP.NET Core application. Strongly typed models provide the best developer experience, while ViewBag and ViewData offer convenient shortcuts for simpler scenarios.
